{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "more than 700,000 people die by suicide every year", "source_url": "https://www.who.int/news/item/17-06-2021-one-in-100-deaths-is-by-suicide", "note": "WHO states 'In 2019, more than 700 000 people died by suicide: one in every 100 deaths' based on Global Health Estimates data."}, {"claim_snippet": "more than 700,000 people die by suicide every year", "source_url": "https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/suicide", "note": "WHO fact sheet states 'Every year more than 700 000 people take their own life' and elsewhere updates to 'More than 720 000 people die due to suicide every year.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "more than 700,000 people die by suicide every year", "source_url": "https://www.paho.org/en/one-100-deaths-suicide", "note": "PAHO/WHO repeats the same WHO 2019 figure: 'more than 700 000 people died by suicide: one in every 100 deaths.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "more than 700,000 people die by suicide every year", "source_url": "https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/suicide-rates-are-higher-in-men-than-women", "note": "Secondary source repeating WHO figure: 'Globally, more than 700,000 people die from suicide every year.'"}], "origin_trace": "Earliest identifiable source is WHO's own 17 June 2021 news release 'One in 100 deaths is by suicide' (who.int), which reports that in 2019 more than 700,000 people died by suicide globally, based on WHO Global Health Estimates. This figure has since been carried forward in WHO's ongoing suicide fact sheet, with a newer WHO fact sheet slightly updating the figure to 'more than 720,000' in more recent years, but '700,000' remains an official WHO-cited figure and is still used by WHO itself in current materials.", "reasoning": "The claim's figure and attribution match the WHO's own published statistic almost exactly, worded as 'more than 700,000 people die by suicide every year,' which is language WHO itself uses. There is minor nuance: the original 2021 release ties the figure to the year 2019, and a newer WHO fact sheet has updated the estimate slightly upward to 'more than 720,000,' but WHO's own materials still also state the 700,000 figure as a general 'every year' framing, matching the claim closely. No causal overreach or population distortion is present since the claim simply restates WHO's global annual estimate. Given that this is a direct, near-verbatim match to WHO's own primary statements, the claim is well supported."}

{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.spring.org.uk/2023/02/what-percentage-communication-nonverbal.php", "note": "States the 93% nonverbal figure is a myth; the original Mehrabian experiments (55% facial + 38% vocal = 93% nonverbal) 'only applied to communicating attitudes and feelings,' not all communication."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mehrabian", "note": "Describes Mehrabian's actual finding as the '7%-38%-55% Rule' for words, tone, and body language in conveying feelings/attitudes, not a blanket 93% figure for 'all communication.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://law.temple.edu/aer/2021/05/03/brain-lessons-the-seven-percent-delusion/", "note": "Notes the equation was 'derived from experiments dealing with communications of feelings and attitudes' and that 'unless a communicator is talking about their feelings or attitudes, these equations are not applicable.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.watermarklearning.com/blog/correcting-the-mehrabian-myth-with-words-only/", "note": "Confirms the 7-38-55 rule 'only applies to very specific communication circumstances' involving conflicting emotional cues, not general communication."}], "origin_trace": "Original source: Albert Mehrabian's studies (Mehrabian & Ferris 1967; Mehrabian & Wiener 1967), summarized on Wikipedia and analyzed by multiple secondary sources (PsyBlog, Temple Law AER, Watermark Learning). Mehrabian's experiments measured how people judge a speaker's feelings/attitudes (like-dislike) when facial expression, tone, and words conflict, yielding the 7%-38%-55% breakdown that sums nonverbal channels to 93%. The claim generalizes this narrow, specific experimental finding to 'all human communication.'", "reasoning": "Multiple independent sources trace the 93% figure to Mehrabian's 1967 studies, but all agree the finding was restricted to judging inconsistent verbal/nonverbal cues about feelings and attitudes, not communication broadly. The claim strips out this critical scope limitation and asserts a universal rule ('all human communication'), which Mehrabian himself and subsequent scholars have explicitly rejected as a misapplication. Because the figure is real but the framing is fundamentally distorted in scope and generality, this is best classified as not supported when taken as a general claim about all communication, since the population/context has been broadened far beyond what the original research measured."}

{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Traces the 20,000 vs 7,000 figure to Louann Brizendine's 2006 book 'The Female Brain,' not a rigorous study; Scientific American reports this claim as false."}, {"claim_snippet": "origin of the 20,000/7,000 figures", "source_url": "https://psychology-spot.com/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Reports a University of Pennsylvania researcher traced the figures to an unsourced 1993 marriage counselor's pamphlet, with no scientific basis."}, {"claim_snippet": "a study found... women speak... men speak only", "source_url": "https://www.npr.org/2007/07/05/11762186/study-men-talk-just-as-much-as-women", "note": "The actual peer-reviewed study (Mehl et al., Science, 2007) found women spoke ~16,000 words/day and men ~15,000-16,000/day, a difference NPR describes as not statistically significant."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://time.com/2992051/women-talk-more-study/", "note": "Time confirms the 20,000/7,000 statistic is widely cited in self-help books but is unsourced folklore, contrasting it with the 2007 study's ~16,215 vs ~15,669 finding."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak... men speak only", "source_url": "https://www.jpost.com/science/science-around-the-world/article-840587", "note": "Cites a 2007 study finding men and women 'do not differ in daily word usage, each speaking about 16,000 words per day.'"}], "origin_trace": "The earliest traceable source of the 20,000-vs-7,000 figure is an unsourced 1993 marriage-counseling pamphlet, later popularized by Louann Brizendine's 2006 book 'The Female Brain.' The only rigorous peer-reviewed study on this topic (Mehl et al., published in Science, 2007, using wearable recorders on ~400 students) found men and women speak roughly the same amount, about 16,000 words per day each, with no statistically significant difference.", "reasoning": "The claim attributes the 20,000/7,000 figure to 'a study,' but no such study exists; the numbers originate from an unsourced self-help pamphlet and were popularized by a non-peer-reviewed book. The actual controlled study on daily word counts (Mehl et al. 2007) directly contradicts the claim, finding both sexes speak comparably (~16,000 words/day) with the difference not statistically significant. Multiple independent science journalism sources (NPR, Scientific American, Time, Jerusalem Post) confirm this figure is a debunked myth. Therefore the claim is not supported by any credible original source and is contradicted by the best available data."}
